# Question 1: Political Efficacy in China and Mexico
## Question 1.1

*We begin by analyzing the self-assessment question. Plot the distribution of responses separately for China and
Mexico using bar plots, where the vertical axis is the proportion of respondents. In addition, compute the mean
response for each country. Which country’s respondents have a higher degree of political efficacy? Does this seem
plausible when Mexican citizens voted out the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) after more than 70 years of
rule and Chinese citizens have not been able to vote in a fair election to date?*

```{r q1-1}
vignettes <- read.csv("~/Dropbox/My Mac (Apple’s MacBook Air)/Desktop/Purdue/Fall 2026/Intro to Research Methods/PS2/vignettes.csv")
# Split dataset into two groups for China and Mexico
china <- subset(vignettes, china == 1)
mexico <- subset(vignettes, china == 0)

# Three steps: count, convert to proportions, plot
# Count and convert to proportion
tab_china <- prop.table(table(china$self))
tab_china
tab_mexico <- prop.table(table(mexico$self))
tab_mexico

# Make a plot for China
scale_labels_china <- c("No say\n at all", "Little say", "Some say", "A lot\n of say",
                  "Unlimited say")
barplot(tab_china,
        names = scale_labels_china,
        xlab  = "Response category",
        ylab  = "Proportion of respondents",
        main  = "The distribution of self-assessment responses in China")

# Make a plot for Mexico
scale_labels_mexico <- c("No say\n at all", "Little say", "Some say", "A lot\n of say",
                  "Unlimited say")
barplot(tab_mexico,
        names = scale_labels_mexico,
        xlab  = "Response category",
        ylab  = "Proportion of respondents",
        main  = "The distribution of self-assessment responses in Mexico")

# Compute mean response for each country
mean(china$self) # for China
mean(mexico$self) # for Mexico

```

**Answer.**
China's respondents have a higher degree of political efficacy than Mexico's 
ones (2.62 > 1.83). The results seem plausible, because the "self" variable 
measures self-reported scores of political efficacy among citizens or their 
perceived political efficacy in terms of perception that is different from the 
actual political influence of citizens on the government or the election. 
A Chinese individual can feel capable of engaging in politics, but the political
system offers him much less opportunity to participate in fair elections that 
represent his political will. 

## Question 1.2

*We examine the possibility that any difference in the levels of efficacy between Mexican and Chinese respondents is
due to the difference in their age distributions. Create histograms for the age variable separately for Mexican and
Chinese respondents. Add a vertical line representing the median age of the respondents for each country. In
addition, use a Quantile-Quantile plot to compare the two age distributions. What differences in age distribution do
you observe between the two countries? Are the variables normally distributed or is there skewness? Answer this by
interpreting each plot.*

```{r q1-2}
# Make a histogram for China and add a vertical line
hist(china$age,
     freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Years of age",
     main = "Distribution of Respondents' Age in China")

med_china <- median(china$age)
abline(v = med_china, lty = "dashed", lwd = 2, col = "blue")
text(x = med_china, y = 0.03, labels = "median", pos = 4, col = "blue")

# Make a histogram for Mexico and add a vertical line
hist(mexico$age,
     freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Years of age",
     main = "Distribution of Respondents' Age in Mexico")

med_mexico <- median(mexico$age)
abline(v = med_mexico, lty = "dashed", lwd = 2, col = "red")
text(x = med_mexico, y = 0.03, labels = "median", pos = 4, col = "red")

# Make Q-Q plot to compare the two age distributions
qqplot(mexico$age, china$age,
       xlab = "Age: Mexico",
       ylab = "Age: China",
       xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100),
       main = "Age distributions compared")
abline(0, 1)

```

**Answer.**
Looking at histograms, in China, the distritbution of age is not normally 
distributed and slightly right-skewed (median = 45 < mean = 46.72). In Mexico, 
the distritbution of age is not normally distributed and fairly right-skewed 
(median = 35 < mean = 37.93) with a few outliers. Looking at the Q-Q plot,
the distribution of age in both countries is not normal, most of data points 
are above the straight line. The slope of the age distribution is greater than
45 degree, indicating that the respondents' age in China is more dispersed than 
the respondents' age in Mexico.

## Question 1.3

*One problem of the self-assessment question is that survey respondents may interpret the question differently. For
example, two respondents who choose the same response category may be facing quite different political situations
and hence may interpret “A lot of say” differently. To address this problem, we rank a respondent’s answer to the
self-assessment question relative to the same respondent’s answer to a vignette question. Compute the proportion
of respondents, again separately for China and Mexico, who rank themselves (according to the self-assessment
question) as having less say in the government’s decisions than Moses (the last vignette). How does the result of this
analysis differ from that of the previous analysis? Give a brief interpretation of the result.*

```{r q1-3}
# Compute the proportion of respondents rank themselves having less say than 
# Moses
mean(china$self < china$moses)   
mean(mexico$self < mexico$moses)
```

**Answer.**
While the previous analysis (in Question 1) indicates that China's respondents 
have a higher degree of political efficacy than Mexico's ones (2.62 > 1.83), 
the proportion of those Chinese respondents who rank themselves having less say 
than Moses is greater than that of Mexican respondents (0.56 > 0.25). This 
suggests that though the Chinese respondents' self-perception of participating 
in politics is higher than the Mexican respondents' one, more Chinese 
individuals feel that their sayings possibly do not have an influence on the 
government, so they would rather suffer in silence. 

## Question 1.4

*Restrict the data to survey respondents who ranked these three vignettes in the expected order (i.e., Alison
≥Jane≥Moses). Now create a variable that represents how respondents rank themselves relative to each vignette.
This variable should be equal to 1 if a respondent ranks themself lower than Moses, 2 if ranked the same as Moses
or higher than Moses but lower than Jane, 3 if ranked the same as Jane or higher than Jane but lower than Alison,
and 4 if ranked as high as Alison or higher. Create the bar plots of this new variable as in Question 1. The vertical
axis should represent the proportion of respondents for each response category. Also, compute the mean value of
this new variable separately for China and Mexico. Give a brief interpretation of the result by comparing these
results with those obtained in Question 1.*

```{r q1-4}
# First keep only respondents whose vignette ratings are internally consistent:
vignettes_ok <- subset(vignettes, alison >= jane & jane >= moses)
nrow(vignettes)
nrow(vignettes_ok)   # the number of dropped observations

# Build a new variable in the expected order, earlier conditions ruled out 
# higher categories
vignettes_ok$rank4 <- ifelse(vignettes_ok$self >= vignettes_ok$alison, 4,
                ifelse(vignettes_ok$self >= vignettes_ok$jane, 3,
                ifelse(vignettes_ok$self >= vignettes_ok$moses, 2, 1)))
                
# Count and convert to proportion
tab_vig_ok <- prop.table(table(vignettes_ok$rank4))
tab_vig_ok

# Make a plot for the new variable
scale_labels_vig_ok <- c("Lower than\n Moses", "Moses to\n below Jane",
                         "Jane to\n below Alison", "Alison\n or higher")
barplot(tab_vig_ok,
        names = scale_labels_vig_ok,
        xlab  = "Response category",
        ylab  = "Proportion of respondents",
        main  = "The distribution of self-assessment relative to each vignette")

# Compute mean response for each country
tapply(vignettes_ok$rank4, vignettes_ok$china, mean) #vignettes_ok$rank4 = var; 
                                                    # china = group by country

```
```

**Answer.**
While China's respondents have a higher degree of political efficacy than 
Mexico's ones (2.62 > 1.83), the proportion of respondents who rank themselves 
relative to each vignette in China is lower than the proportion of those 
in Mexico (2.15 < 2.93). 

## Question 1.5

*Is the problem identified above more or less severe among older respondents when compared to younger ones?
Consider the previous question for those who are 40 years or older and those who are younger than 40 years. What
are your conclusions with respect to these two groups of respondents? Relate your discussion to your finding for
Question 2.*

```{r q1-5}
# Build a new variable for two age groups
vignettes_ok$age_group <- ifelse(vignettes_ok$age >= 40, 1, 0)

# Compute the difference between China and Mexico in terms of age groups
tapply(vignettes_ok$rank4, list(vignettes_ok$china, vignettes_ok$age_group), 
        mean, na.rm = TRUE)

## Need to compare both the raw self-assessment and adjusted measures within the two age groups to compare with earlier finding
# Raw self-assessment
vignettes$age_group <- ifelse(vignettes$age >= 40, 1, 0)

# Compute the difference between China and Mexico in terms of age groups
tapply(vignettes$self, list(vignettes$china, vignettes$age_group), 
        mean, na.rm = TRUE)

```

**Answer.**
For self-assessment, among older respondents, the mean value of respondents' 
self-ranking for Mexico is 1.77, and China is 2.75. Among younger respondents 
(those are below 40), the mean value is 1.85 for Mexico, and 2.39 for China. 
The difference between older respondents is higher compared to younger ones (0.98)


Among older respondents (those are 40 years old or older), the mean value of 
respondents' ranking three vignettes in the expected order for Mexico is 2.92, 
and China is 2.20 . Among younger respondents (those are below 40), the mean 
value is 2.93 for Mexico, and 2.04 for China. Thus, the difference between 
China and Mexico is higher among younger respondents, compared with older ones 
(2.93 - 2.04 = 0.89 > 2.92 - 2.20 = 0.72). This implies that the China-Mexico
difference in political efficacy is more severe for younger respondents. As 
shown in the QQ plot in Question 2, Chinese respondents appear to be older than
Mexican ones due to more dispersed data points for the China sample. The 
difference in political efficacy between two countries doesn't seem to be 
explained by the difference in age groups. 

## Question 1.6

*Researchers interviewed 430 respondents in China (across 2 provinces) and 551 in Mexico (across 3 provinces).
What is the final sample size for China and Mexico in the data? Discuss the potential reasons behind the
discrepancy. Are there any biases that could be affecting the results? If so, which ones?*

```{r q1-6}
# Check the final sample size for each country and the total
table(vignettes$china)
dim(vignettes)
```

**Answer.**
The final sample size in the data is 781 in which there are 283 respondents in 
China, and 498 respondents in Mexico. There are fewer 200 respondents than the 
number of those who are actually interviewed. There are some potential reasons
for the discrepancy. First, some respondents, who did not complete some specific 
questions (having missing answers), are exlucded from the analysis. Second, 
respondents, who provide insufficient information about some key variables, 
such as age, country, and vignette responses, are also dropped during listwise 
deletion. Third, during data-cleaning process, reseachers may remove some 
observations due to their invalidity. 

Yes, there are some biases that could affect the results, such as selection 
bias and nonresponse bias. First, if a certain type of respondents, who are 
categorized in a specific group of age or country, are excluded from the study, 
leading to the disproportion of final sample size that is no longer 
representative of the population. This may result in a biased study. Second, a 
certain group of respondents may refuse to complete the interview. Thus, the 
remaining observations may not represent the entire population. 


## Question 1.7

*Plot the histogram of the variable `age` in the vignettes.csv data and describe the shape of the distribution. Is `age` a
categorical or continuous variable? Now create a new variable called lage and store the log transformation of the
age variable. Plot the distribution of `lage` and describe the shape. Is using log transformation helpful?*

```{r q1-7}
# Make a histogram for the 'age' variable
hist(vignettes$age,
     freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Years of age",
     main = "Distribution of Respondents' Age")

# Create a new variable for lage
vignettes$lage <- log(vignettes$age)

# Make a histogram for the 'lage' variable
hist(vignettes$lage,
     freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Logged Age",
     main = "Distribution of Respondents' Age")
```

**Answer.**
The distribution of the age variable is not normally distributed and 
right-skewed. Age is continuous variable. 

The distribution of logged age is relatively normally distributed and 
symmetrical. Using log transformation is helpful.

# Question 2: Sources of Empathy in the Circuit Courts

## Question 2.1

*Load the “dbj.csv file”. Find how many judges there are in the dataset, as well as the gender and party composition
of our dataset. Is the party composition different for male and female judges? Additionally, note that our outcome
in this exercise will be the proportion of pro-feminist rulings. What is the range of this variable (progressive.vote)?*

```{r q2-1}
# Load data
dbj <- read.csv("~/Dropbox/My Mac (Apple’s MacBook Air)/Desktop/Purdue/Fall 2026/Intro to Research Methods/PS2/dbj.csv")
dim(dbj)
length(dbj$name)

# Find the number of female and male judges
length(dbj$woman[dbj$woman == "0"]) # men
length(dbj$woman[dbj$woman == "1"]) # women

# Find party composition
length(dbj$republican[dbj$republican == "1"]) # Republican judges
length(dbj$republican[dbj$republican == "0"]) # Democratic judges

# Create a two-way table to check party composition across genders
table(dbj$republican, dbj$woman)
prop.table(table(dbj$republican, dbj$woman), 2) # compute % each column

# Find range of 'pro-feminist rulings' variable
range(dbj$progressive.vote, na.rm = TRUE)
```

**Answer.**
There are 224 judges in the dataset. There are 186 male judges, and 38 female 
judges. There are 121 Republican judges, and 103 Democratic judges. 

Party composition differs for male and female judges. Among male judges, 40.86% 
are Democrats, and 59.14% are Republicans. Among female judges, 71.05% are 
Democrats, and 28.95% are Republicans. 

The 'pro-feminist rulings' variable ranges from 0 to 1.

## Question 2.2

*Next, we consider differences between some groups. For each of the four groups (Republican men/women,
Democratic men/women) defined by gender and partisanship, create a boxplot (using a single command) that
illustrates the differences in progressive.vote. Briefly interpret the results of the analysis. For example, do any of
the results surprise you? Does it appear that partisanship, gender, or both contribute to progressive voting
patterns? Should we interpret any of these effects causally? Why or why not?*

```{r q2-2}
# Create a boxplot
boxplot(progressive.vote ~ woman + republican, data = dbj,
        names = c("Dem. men", "Dem. women", "Rep. men", "Rep. women"),
        xlab = "Gender and party",
        ylab = "Proportion of pro-feminist rulings",
        main  = "Pro-feminist rulings by gender and party")
        
# Re-check if groups match their corresponding median values
tapply(dbj$progressive.vote, list(dbj$republican, dbj$woman), 
        median, na.rm = TRUE)
```


**Answer.**
Yes, the results are surprising that the group of male Democratic judges tend 
to have pro-feminist voting behavior due to its highest median of 0.50. 
Meanwhile, the group of female Republican judges has the lowest proportion of 
pro-feminist rulings with a median of 0.33. 

For both men and women, Democratic judges have higher median proportions of  
pro-feminist rulings than Republican ones. Thus, partisanship shows big
differences. However, gender has some differences, but smaller. Among Democrats,
men have a higher median than women, and among Republicans, men and women have 
similar medians. Therefore, partisanship has a greater contribution to 
progressive voting patterns. 

We shouldn't interpret these effects as causally because judges are not randomly
assigned to partisanship and gender. Moreover, there are many other factors that 
possibly cause the difference in pro-feminist rulings, such as ideology, age, 
and judicial experiences. 



## Question 2.3

*Create a new binary variable which takes a value of 1 if a judge has at least one child (that is, any children at all), 0
otherwise. Then, use this variable to answer the following questions. Are Republicans and Democrats equally likely
to be parents (that is, have at least one child)? Do judges with children vote differently than judges without? If so,
how are they different? Do republican and democratic parents vote differently on feminist issues?*

```{r q2-3}
# Create a binary variable
dbj$parent <- ifelse(dbj$child >= 1, 1, 0)

# Compute the proportion of parents within each party
table(dbj$republican, dbj$parent)
prop.table(table(dbj$republican, dbj$parent), 1) # pick 1 (rows) to compute %
                                                  # partisanship

# Compute the proportion of pro-feminist voting within parent and non-parent
# groups
tapply(dbj$progressive.vote, dbj$parent, mean, na.rm = TRUE) # for the voting comparisons                                                         #should use mean rather than the median

# Compute the proportion of pro-feminist voting between 2 parties 
# within parent groups
tapply(dbj$progressive.vote[dbj$parent == "1"], 
      dbj$republican[dbj$parent == "1"], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

**Answer.**
88.35% Democrats are parents, and 89.26% Republicans are parents. The difference
is small. Thus, Republicans and Democrats are relatively similar in the 
likelihood of being parents. Republicans are slightly more likely to be parents. 

Judges with children vote differently than judges without. Judges with 
children have a slightly lower proportion of pro-feminist voting than those 
without children (0.41 < 0.42). 

Yes, republican and democratic parents vote differently on feminist issues. 
Democrat parents have a higher median proportion of voting on feminist issues 
than Republican ones (0.50 > 0.33). 


## Question 2.4

*What is the difference in the proportion of pro-feminist decisions between judges who have at least one daughter
and those who do not have any? Compute this difference in two ways; (1) using the entire sample, (2) separately by
the number of children judges have (only considering judges that have 3 children or less). What assumptions are
required for us to interpret these differences as causal estimates?*

```{r q2-4}
# Create a binary variable for 2 groups of judges who have at least 1 daughter
dbj$daughter <- ifelse(dbj$girls >= 1, 1, 0)

# Use the entire sample to compute the difference in the proportion of 
# pro-feminist decisions
mean(dbj$progressive.vote[dbj$daughter == "1"]) -
    mean(dbj$progressive.vote[dbj$daughter == "0"])

tapply(dbj$progressive.vote, dbj$daughter, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

### Separately by the number of children judges have, then compute the difference
### in the proportion of pro-femnist decisions while holding the number of child
### constant
# Create a variable for the sample of judges with 3 children or less
dbj.3 <- dbj[dbj$child <= 3, ]

# Compute the difference in the proportion for those who have 1 child
mean(dbj.3$progressive.vote[dbj.3$child == "1" & dbj.3$daughter == "1"]) -
    mean(dbj.3$progressive.vote[dbj.3$child == "1" & dbj.3$daughter == "0"])
    
# Compute the difference in the proportion for those who have 2 children
mean(dbj.3$progressive.vote[dbj.3$child == "2" & dbj.3$daughter == "1"]) -
    mean(dbj.3$progressive.vote[dbj.3$child == "2" & dbj.3$daughter == "0"])
    
# Compute the difference in the proportion for those who have 3 children
mean(dbj.3$progressive.vote[dbj.3$child == "3" & dbj.3$daughter == "1"]) -
    mean(dbj.3$progressive.vote[dbj.3$child == "3" & dbj.3$daughter == "0"])

```

**Answer.**
For the entire sample, the proportion of pro-feminist decisions is 6.4 
percentage points higher among judges who have at least one daughter than among
those who don't. 

Separately, among judges having 1 child, the proportion of pro-feminist 
decisions is 24.08 percentage points higher among judges having at least one
daughter than those having no daughter. 

Among judges having 2 children, the proportion of pro-feminist decisions is 
8.47 percentage points higher among judges having at least one daughter than 
those having no daughter. 

Among judges having 3 children, the proportion of pro-feminist decisions is 
18.93 percentage points higher among judges having at least one daughter than 
those having no daughter. 

To interpret these differences as causal estimates, we're required some 
assumptions. First, there is no other possible confounding factors, such as age, 
political ideology of judges, judical experiences, or family background that may
affect the possibility of having a daughter and making a judical decision. 

Second, among judges who have the same number of children, it's required that 
having a daughter isn't associated with other factors that determine 
pro-feminist decisions. 

Third, judges are independent from each other in making decisions. One's having 
a daughter doesn't affect the other's pro-feminist decision. 

## Question 2.5

*Next, we are going to consider the design of this study. The original authors assume that conditional on the number
of children a judge has the number of daughters is random (as we did in the previous question). Indeed, this is the
assumption that would justify the analysis of the previous question. For example, among the judges who have two
children, the number of daughters – either 0, 1, or 2 – has nothing to do with the (observed or unobserved) pretreatment
characteristics of judges. Is this assumption reasonable? Is there a scenario under which this assumption
can be violated? Do the data support the assumption?*

### The question asks the number of daughters conditional on number of children, 
### the answer collapses daughter composition into no daughter versus at least one daughter

```{r q2-5}
### To examine if the data supports the assumption, need to test if the 
### pre-treatment characteristics of race and religion among judges remain 
### different systematically across different numbers of daughter while holding
### the number of children constant

## Compare the characteristic of race within each number of children, use 
## the sample of judges with 3 children or less to test

# For judges with 1 child
table(dbj.3$race[dbj.3$child == "1"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "1"])
prop.table(table(dbj.3$race[dbj.3$child == "1"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "1"]), 2)

# For judges with 2 children
table(dbj.3$race[dbj.3$child == "2"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "2"])
prop.table(table(dbj.3$race[dbj.3$child == "2"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "2"]), 2)

# For judges with 3 children
table(dbj.3$race[dbj.3$child == "3"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "3"])
prop.table(table(dbj.3$race[dbj.3$child == "3"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "3"]), 2)

## Compare the characteristic of religion within each number of children, use 
## the sample of judges with 3 children or less to test

# For judges with 1 child
table(dbj.3$religion[dbj.3$child == "1"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "1"])
prop.table(table(dbj.3$religion[dbj.3$child == "1"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "1"]), 2)

# For judges with 2 children
table(dbj.3$religion[dbj.3$child == "2"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "2"])
prop.table(table(dbj.3$religion[dbj.3$child == "2"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "2"]), 2)

# For judges with 3 children
table(dbj.3$religion[dbj.3$child == "3"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "3"])
prop.table(table(dbj.3$religion[dbj.3$child == "3"], dbj.3$daughter[dbj.3$child == "3"]), 2)

```

**Answer.**
This assumption is reasonable. Because the gender of a child isn't determined 
by the judges' control, but biological factors. Therefore, among judges, who 
have the same number of children, with different numbers of daughter, having
similar pre-treatment characteristics. 

This assumption could be violated if the number of daughter is related to
the judges' pre-treatment characteristics, possibly affecting their pro-feminist
voting behavior. For instance, in the contexts of gender-selection and family
preferences, the judges' family, which already have a daughter, may have a 
preference of having a son, and thus they try to have the second child. 
Meanwhile, in the judges' family, which already have a son, they may have no 
attempt to have the second child. Accordingly, among judges with the same 
number of children, the number of daughter is related to the 
judges' pre-treatment characteristics. 

In terms of race and religion, we see that the racial proportion and the 
religious proportion are approximately the same across two groups of daughter 
(no daughter and at least 1 daughter). Thus, this data supports the assumption.
